title: Abacha na Ugba
author: Chioma Adeleke
desc: Shredded dried cassava and fermented oil bean dressed in an emulsion of thirty centilitres of palm oil and two tablespoons of potash — mixed entirely off the stove.
longDesc: Abacha is dried shredded cassava and it has already been through a process before you meet it: the tubers are cooked, sliced with a special grater, soaked in cold water overnight, washed thoroughly and sun-dried. To make the salad you rehydrate it, then dress it with the ncha emulsion — thirty centilitres of palm oil into which potash water is poured, carefully leaving the sediment behind, until the oil turns into a yellow paste. Everything is mixed off the stove, because any heat or water in the pot will break the emulsion. An optional reheat at the end is the only time it sees a flame.
ingredients: 2 tbsp powdered potash (food tenderiser), dissolved in approximately 1 cup cold water
Fish — mackerel, dry fish or stockfish
Salt and dry pepper, to taste
steps: Soak the abacha in cold water to rehydrate it, then drain thoroughly in a colander.
Dissolve the potash in approximately 1 cup of cold water and let the sediment settle.
Pour the red palm oil into a clean dry bowl.
Pour the water from the potash mixture into the oil, making sure not to pour the sediments.
Stir very well and you'll see the oil turn into a yellow paste.
Add the ground crayfish, ground ehu seeds, stock cubes, dry pepper and salt, and mix.
Fold in the ugba, the drained abacha, the sliced onion and the fish.
Mix thoroughly, all off the stove.
If you want it warm, reheat to your desired temperature at medium heat.
chefTips: Everything off the stove. The emulsion forms cold and heat is what breaks it — the optional reheat comes after it is fully mixed.
Leave the sediment behind. The instruction is explicit: pour the water from the potash mixture, making sure not to pour the sediments.
The yellow paste is the cue. Red oil going opaque yellow and thickening is the whole technique.
Drain the abacha properly. Wet abacha dilutes the emulsion and the dressing slides off.
Two tablespoons of potash to 30 cl of oil is a much higher alkali load than the ncha recipe's 2 teaspoons to half a cup. Start lower and build if you are unsure.
Ehu is calabash nutmeg — the same spice as ehuru — and a teaspoon of it is what makes abacha taste of abacha.
Garden eggs, sliced, and a handful of utazi are the usual additions if you have them.
commonMistakes: Tipping the potash sediment into the oil.
Using abacha that is still wet.
Adding the potash water all at once.
Leaving out the ehu, which flattens the whole dish.
sources: Adapted from 'African Salad (Abacha and Ugba)', All Nigerian Recipes — no byline on the page, credited to the site. Quantities as printed: 3 handfuls abacha; 2 cups ugba (ukpaka); 30 cl red palm oil; 2 tablespoons powdered potash (food tenderizer), dissolved in approximately 1 cup cold water; fish (mackerel/dry fish/stockfish) — no quantity; 1 large onion; salt and dry pepper to taste; 4 tablespoons ground crayfish; 2 stock cubes; 1 teaspoon ground ehu seeds. Yield not specified.

WHAT ABACHA IS BEFORE IT IS A SALAD, as described on the same page: 'The cassava tubers are cooked till done then sliced with a special grater. The sliced cassava is then soaked in cold water overnight, washed thoroughly and dried under the sun.'

And on ugba, from the same page: 'made from oil bean seeds. These seeds are cooked for several hours then sliced, washed and left to ferment a little bit.' NOTE that 'a little bit' is the only duration given — no number at all. For a properly documented ugba fermentation with a measurable endpoint see NGA057.

THE EMULSION STEPS, verbatim: 'Pour the water from the potash mixture, making sure not to pour the sediments' into the oil, then 'Stir very well and you'll see the oil turn into a yellow paste.' All mixing is off the stove, with an optional final reheat 'to your desired temperature at medium heat'.

DISAGREEMENT on the alkali load, not reconciled: 2 tablespoons of potash to 30 cl of oil here, against 2 teaspoons to 1/2 cup in the Afrolems ncha (NGA054). Those are substantially different concentrations and both are published by named sources.

COUNTER-FINDING, flagged: this page does NOT use the word 'ncha' despite describing the identical emulsion. The technique is universal across the sources; the name is attested only by 1Q Food Platter and Afrolems.

Abacha is the most divergent dish in the corpus consulted — sources disagree on the alkali and its quantity, on whether the palm oil is heated at all, and on what else goes in. Nothing is averaged here.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. The emulsion will separate; stir it back.
reheating: Gentle warmth only, after mixing. Do not cook it.
healthBenefits: Fermented oil bean is high in protein and B vitamins.
Red palm oil supplies carotenoids and vitamin E.
No cooking, so the nutrients in the fresh additions survive.
culturalNote: Abacha is bar food and market food, sold in a bowl with a cold drink and eaten at any hour. It is also one of the few genuinely raw-assembled dishes in the Nigerian repertoire — nothing is cooked at the point of making it, because the whole thing depends on an emulsion that heat would destroy. The cooking happened days earlier, when the cassava was boiled, sliced, soaked and dried.
